title: Yitro: the last word is inside (Exodus 20:14)
hook: the final commandment, not to covet, governs the heart rather than the hands
tomorrow: Mishpatim: straight after Sinai, the details

segments.voice: Yesterday, anochi, the first of the Ten Words: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out. Your line was first, a relationship. Today, the last day of Yitro, and the last of the ten.

Scroll through anyone's feed for five minutes: the kitchen renovation, the beach in Greece, the promotion, the couple who never seem to argue. Nobody stole anything. Nobody lied. And still a phone gets put down by someone feeling a little smaller, wanting what's theirs. Most of the Ten Words are about things you could see someone do or not do: make an idol, work on Shabbat, steal, lie in court. The tenth is different. Nobody can see you break it.
screen: `FIVE MINUTES OF SCROLLING.` → `A LITTLE SMALLER, WANTING MORE.` → `NOBODY CAN SEE IT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, the tenth begins: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house"; then the list: his wife, his servants, his ox, his donkey, anything that belongs to your neighbor. In Hebrew, lo tachmod. The first word was anochi, I, God's own self. The last word reaches into your own self. Abraham ibn Ezra, the medieval Spanish commentator, asked the honest question: how can anyone be commanded not to feel something? Wanting just happens. His answer is a parable. A villager sees a beautiful princess pass by. He doesn't lie awake longing to marry her, because he knows it's simply not his world. In the same way, says Ibn Ezra, a person who truly understands that what's yours is yours by God's gift will stop reaching for what isn't. The wanting quiets down because the frame has changed. The early rabbis and Maimonides read the verse more narrowly in law: you break it when you act on the wanting, pressuring someone until they hand over what's theirs. Deuteronomy adds a second verb, about desire itself. So there's a range of readings, from the hands to the heart. Either way, the list that starts at Sinai ends inside the chest. And with that, Yitro is done: an outsider's wisdom, one heart, eagles' wings, the first word, and the last.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT COVET.` · `LO TACHMOD: INTO THE SELF.` · `IBN EZRA: THE VILLAGER AND PRINCESS.` · `FROM THE HANDS TO THE HEART.` · then, large: `THE LAST WORD IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Name, without scolding yourself, one thing in someone else's life you've quietly been wanting: their house, their job, their marriage, their calm. Then turn to what's actually in your hands right now, a person, a skill, a small comfort, this breath, and hold that instead. If you pray, you can give thanks for one of those things, and let the envy loosen a little.
Yitro. The portion we finish today, whose Ten Words begin with God's I and end inside the human heart.
Your line: the last word is inside. The ten begin with God's I and end in the human heart. That's day three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish law, following the Mekhilta and Maimonides, holds that the command not to covet is broken by acting on the desire, such as pressuring an owner to sell; Jewish ethical writers also treat envy itself as a trait to work on.
